# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Contemporary Narrative Review

## Introduction and Epidemiology

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in the myocardium, producing progressive ventricular wall thickening and stiffening, heart failure, and conduction disease [1]. It is a serious and progressive infiltrative disease caused by the deposition of amyloid fibrils at the cardiac level, due to rare genetic variants in hereditary forms or as a consequence of acquired conditions; thanks to advances in imaging techniques and the possibility of achieving a non-invasive diagnosis, cardiac amyloidosis is now recognized as a more frequent disease than traditionally considered [2]. Two precursor proteins account for the overwhelming majority of cases: transthyretin amyloid and immunoglobulin-derived light chain amyloid [1]. Once regarded as rare, CA is now appreciated as an underdiagnosed contributor to common cardiac syndromes [3]. Wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis accounts for approximately 13% of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) cases and is an underdiagnosed cause that might benefit from specific treatments [4]. In a prospective cohort, among consecutive patients ≥60 years admitted with HFpEF and left ventricular hypertrophy who underwent 99mTc-DPD scintigraphy, 16 of 120 patients (13.3%) showed moderate-to-severe uptake [4]. CA also coexists with calcific aortic stenosis: in 2017 Castaño et al. studied 151 patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis and found 16% to have concomitant ATTR-CA [5], with a subsequent multicentre registry confirming a high prevalence [6].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

CA frequently presents with nonspecific symptoms, leading to substantial diagnostic delay [7]. Accumulation of amyloid fibrils results in ventricular wall thickening and reduced elasticity, manifesting as diastolic dysfunction that progresses into restrictive cardiomyopathy, while infiltration of the conduction system can lead to conduction disease and atrial arrhythmias [8]. Echocardiography raises suspicion, and speckle-tracking imaging is particularly valuable: relative apical sparing of longitudinal strain using two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography is both sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis [9]. The diagnostic work-up centres on distinguishing subtypes, because treatment differs fundamentally [3]. A landmark advance was non-invasive diagnosis with bone scintigraphy: myocardial radiotracer uptake was greater than 99% sensitive and 86% specific for cardiac ATTR amyloid, and the combination of grade 2 or 3 uptake with absence of a monoclonal protein in serum or urine had a specificity and positive predictive value of 100% [10]. Bone scintigraphy thus enables reliable diagnosis of cardiac ATTR amyloidosis without histology in patients who do not have a monoclonal gammopathy [10]. Accordingly, serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light chain assays must accompany imaging to exclude AL amyloidosis [3]. The ESC Working Group position statement provides a structured diagnostic algorithm integrating these modalities [11].

## Disease-Modifying Therapy in ATTR Cardiomyopathy

Transthyretin stabilisation was validated by the pivotal ATTR-ACT trial. Patients with amyloidosis were randomized to tafamidis (n = 264) versus placebo (n = 177), at 80 mg or 20 mg daily [12]. Tafamidis significantly reduced mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations over 30 months, with a 29.5% mortality rate versus 42.9% with placebo (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.51–0.96) [12]. A pooled dose analysis of ATTR-ACT and its long-term extension further supported the higher dose [13]. A next-generation stabiliser then emerged: acoramidis is a high-affinity TTR stabilizer that inhibits dissociation of tetrameric TTR and leads to more than 90% stabilization across the dosing interval [14]. In patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, acoramidis resulted in a significantly better four-step primary hierarchical outcome containing components of mortality, morbidity, and function than placebo [14].

Gene-silencing therapies that reduce hepatic TTR production represent a complementary strategy. In APOLLO-B, administration of patisiran over 12 months resulted in preserved functional capacity in patients with ATTR cardiac amyloidosis [15]. The subcutaneous RNA-interference agent vutrisiran subsequently demonstrated mortality benefit: patients with ATTR-CM have high mortality and morbidity, and vutrisiran reduced the composite of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in HELIOS-B [16]. In the overall population, vutrisiran reduced the risk of all-cause mortality (HR 0.64; 95% CI 0.46–0.88) and cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.67; 95% CI 0.47–0.96) versus placebo [16], with consistent benefit in those already receiving tafamidis [17]. These siRNA approaches build on the foundational APOLLO trial in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy [18], where cardiac subgroup analyses favoured patisiran [19]. The most novel approach is in-vivo genome editing: NTLA-2001 is an in vivo gene-editing therapeutic designed to treat ATTR amyloidosis by reducing serum TTR, based on the CRISPR-Cas9 system comprising a lipid nanoparticle encapsulating mRNA for Cas9 and a single guide RNA targeting TTR [20], producing deep, durable TTR reductions in early-phase study [21].

## AL Amyloidosis Treatment

In AL amyloidosis, a clonal plasma-cell disorder, therapy targets the underlying clone. The phase 3 ANDROMEDA trial added daratumumab to standard bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone [22]. Survival free from major organ deterioration or hematologic progression was longer in the daratumumab group (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.36–0.93, P = 0.02) [22], with higher cardiac and renal response rates [23]; most of the deaths during the trial were due to amyloidosis-related cardiomyopathy [22], underscoring that cardiac involvement drives prognosis [24]. Anti-fibril therapies are emerging to complement clone-directed treatment [25].

## Prognosis and Future Directions

Cardiac involvement remains the principal determinant of survival in systemic amyloidosis [24,26]. Advancements in cardiac imaging and increased physician awareness have improved diagnosis over the past decade; cardiac involvement carries a poor prognosis, making early detection essential to implement treatments that can alter the disease course and improve outcomes [27]. Contemporary reviews emphasise that early recognition—through biomarkers, multimodality imaging, and increasingly artificial-intelligence-enhanced tools—is the key bottleneck [28,29]. Cardiac amyloidosis is a progressive, underdiagnosed condition caused by deposition of misfolded proteins forming amyloid fibrils that impair cardiac structure and function [30], and the expanding therapeutic armamentarium makes timely diagnosis more consequential than ever [3].
